records.notes: Error-path tier, Feature-installation stage, failing EARLIER than the install-script case: two local Features whose `dependsOn` entries name each other, so no installation order exists. Every individual record is well-formed and configuration read accepts on both sides; the contradiction only appears once the dependency graph is resolved. Paired with the failing-`install.sh` case deliberately — one fails inside an install, the other before any install runs, and an implementation can propagate one while defaulting the other to declaration order and installing both Features anyway. Both sides fail (verified against oracle 0.87.0).

Error-path tier, Feature-installation stage: a local Feature whose `install.sh` exits 29. Configuration read accepts on both sides — a Feature reference is just a key, and nothing reads the install script until it runs — and the failure appears while the Feature is being layered into the image, which is why the declared phase is `build`: on BOTH implementations Features are installed by a Docker build over the base image, so there is no separate install phase for the closed failure-phase set to name. The claim under test is that the failure PROPAGATES: swallowing it would produce a container that looks complete and is missing the Feature, which no success-path case can distinguish. Both sides fail (verified against oracle 0.87.0).

Error-path tier, container-creation stage: `runArgs` carries `--cpus not-a-number`. The document is a well-formed array of strings and both CLIs read it without complaint — `runArgs` is passed through to the runtime verbatim by design, so neither can know the value is bad. The daemon rejects it at create time, after the image is resolved and before any container exists. Chosen over a malformed-config input precisely because nothing upstream of the daemon could have caught it, which is what makes it a later-STAGE failure rather than a slow configuration error. Both sides fail (verified against oracle 0.87.0).

Error-path tier, container-creation stage: a bind mount whose SOURCE path does not exist on the host. The mount string parses, the target is sane, and configuration read echoes it on both sides; only the daemon, at create time, can observe that the source is absent. Distinct from the `runArgs` case in where the rejection comes from — an argument the runtime CLI refuses to parse versus a request the daemon refuses to satisfy — and the two are worth pinning separately because a CLI can validate its own argv construction without ever asking the daemon. Both sides fail (verified against oracle 0.87.0).

FR-040 boundary class for `up`: every collection-valued field present and empty. An empty `features` map, an empty `runArgs` and an empty `mounts` are each a plausible place to emit an argument with nothing after it, which fails at container creation rather than at configuration read.

The COMPOSE half of `bhv-up-container-env-merge-precedence`, which is stated over "the created container" and not over one container shape. Its single-container twin `case-up-env-merge-precedence` could not have caught the compose defect: `commands/up/compose.rs` built the service's environment from `config.container_env` plus CLI `--remote-env` and never read `feature_build.combined_env`, so a Feature's `containerEnv` was baked into the extended image and then dropped from the compose service's `environment:` block. Fixed in 8772e7c; this case is the evidence (#374).

The same three variables as the twin, for the same reason: `CONF_LAYER` is declared by BOTH layers and must take the configuration's value, while `CONF_ONLY_CONFIG` and `CONF_ONLY_FEATURE` are declared by one layer each. Without the feature-only variable, a regression that made the configuration win by DROPPING the Feature layer entirely — which is precisely the compose defect — would pass.

Covers the high-risk triple `hrt-up-compose-single-feature-restart`. The second `up` begins with the Compose project already running, so the declared `first-create-vs-restart` relationship is the oracle: re-entry must reattach to the project it created rather than stand up a second one. The process-graph channel is what makes a duplicated service container visible — an exit code cannot show it, and the observation captures EVERY container matching the workspace label for exactly that reason.

#448 and #462 together. The single marker line pins all FOUR cells of #448's matrix at once: the hook ran, it ran as the image-metadata `remoteUser`, the image's `remoteEnv` reached it, and the workspace's did too. `remoteUser`, the hook and `META_ENV` live ONLY in the service image's `devcontainer.metadata` label; `WS_ENV` only in the workspace's `remoteEnv`.

Measured against the pinned 0.87.0 before either fix was written: the reference's compose `up` wrote `metauser from-image-metadata from-workspace-config`; deacon wrote no file at all. `up`'s compose path never called `merge_image_metadata_after_image_ready`, and its post-create exec passed no user and an empty env, which is why the workspace's own `remoteEnv` had been missing too.

The observation is the FILE, not the exit code: before the fix nothing was written and the status still said 0.

The fourth cell — the hook's USER — is measured HERE, and its history is why this case is worth reading. The fixture image pins `metauser` to uid 1234 while the workspace is a bind mount of a host directory the runner owns, so the hook can only write once its uid has been remapped to the HOST's. That is `updateRemoteUserUID`, and deacon applied it on the single-container path only until #462 — the reference builds a derived `<image>-uid` image and points the service at it through its generated override; deacon now remaps in the running container through the same `apply_user_mapping` its single-container path has always used, an identical observable by a different mechanism. This case's FIRST revision declared `remoteUser` and passed locally purely because the dev container's uid and `adduser`'s first free uid were both 1000; on GitHub's runners it failed with `Permission denied`, which is how #462 was found. Its second revision dropped `remoteUser` to keep a #448 regression distinguishable from a uid coincidence. With #462 fixed the coincidence is gone from the verdict entirely — 1234 never matches a plausible host uid — so the cell is back, and a regression in EITHER fix fails this case on every host.

The marker records `whoami`, not `id -u`: the remapped uid is the HOST's and so differs between a dev box and a CI runner, which would make a fixed assertion a statement about the host. The remap is measured by the file existing at all; the user, by its name.

The hook is the STRING form, deliberately: deacon's compose post-create runs `postCreateCommand` only when it is a string, and the array/object forms and every other phase are a separate pre-existing gap on this path (#460). Keeping the string form leaves this case measuring the metadata merge and the uid remap and nothing else.

No spec-expectation twin: the fixture's base is a `:local` image built from its sibling Dockerfile by `scripts/parity/prepull-fixture-images.sh`, which only the nightly and release lanes run — so a Docker-lane twin would fail on the PR lane for a missing image rather than for a divergence (the same reason `case-run-user-commands-image-metadata-differential` is differential-only). The direction is pinned instead by the `assertion` carried HERE, evaluated against deacon's side on top of the comparison.

Only `chan-exit-code` and `chan-file-content` are observed. `chan-container-state` would drag in the whole compose project-name / label tolerance set that `case-up-compose-project-resources-differential` already carries, none of which is what this case is about.

#460. A compose `up` ran `postCreateCommand` only in its STRING form and queued no other phase, because `up`'s compose path carried its own post-create exec instead of calling the lifecycle engine the single-container path uses. Measured against oracle 0.87.0 on this fixture before the fix: the reference ran all six commands and deacon ran NONE of them — `postCreateCommand` here is the array form, so the old `as_str()` yielded None and nothing was queued at all. Both sides exited 0 either way, so the marker files are the entire observation.

One fixture pins four things at once: WHICH phases run (onCreate, updateContent, postCreate, postStart, postAttach — five, where the old path had one), in WHAT order (the four sequential phases append to one file, so the line order is the phase order), in WHICH command form (string, array and object all appear), and that the object form runs EVERY named command.

The two `postStart` named commands write their OWN files rather than appending to the shared log, for the reason `case-up-lifecycle-object-form` gives: the spec does not order named commands, so asserting them inside one file would pin an order neither CLI promises. The sequential phases can share a file precisely because their order IS promised.

The Compose counterpart of the image-backed Docker-channel case, and the third covering case for `chan-image` and `chan-process-graph` (SC-005's floor). Two claims a Compose `up` can only make on those channels. `chan-image`: the service container is created from the image the Compose file DECLARES (`alpine:3.19`) and still carries deacon's `devcontainer.*` identity alongside Compose's own labels — delegation to Compose without losing identity, which a derived-image substitution would break. `chan-process-graph`: both mounts the service declares are present with their SHAPE — the workspace bind and the named volume — which is what distinguishes a service brought up from its Compose definition from one created directly. The volume's `source` is deliberately not pinned: it is the daemon's `/var/lib/docker/volumes/<project>_...` path and the project name is workspace-derived, so pinning it would assert the temp directory rather than the graph. The network is left out for the same reason (`<project>_default`).

Declarative Docker-backed spec-expectation case (022-conformance-runner US5): `deacon up` in an ISOLATED external temp workspace (collision-resistant, guaranteed cleanup) exercises all four Docker channels — chan-image (deacon stamps devcontainer.source), chan-injected-process (containerEnv CONF_TOKEN injected), chan-process-graph (mount/network/volume graph captured), chan-temporal (container running). Image pinned to alpine:3.19 (V18). The chan-process-graph assertion was an empty `jsonSubset: {}` until 024 US6 — which matches ANY graph, so the channel was inert by construction: the case declared it, observed it, and could not fail on it. It now pins the workspace bind (source, type, read-write) and the network the container joined, which is the graph's headline claim and what reg-process-graph-workspace-mount-vanished perturbs.

Covers the high-risk triple `hrt-up-dockerfile-extends-chain-absent`. The `build.dockerfile` is declared by the PARENT document, so the build context has to be resolved relative to the directory of the file that declared it rather than the child's. Getting that wrong fails the build outright, which is why the exit code is a sufficient observable here and a differential is worth the reference run. The 024 live run showed the differential is one-sided: deacon builds and the REFERENCE fails, because oracle 0.87.0 has no `extends` support at all. That is the already-recorded deacon extension (ext-extends-resolution) surfacing in `up` rather than in `read-configuration`, so the case links bhv-readconfig-extends-merged and scopes a tolerance to the exit code. deacon's own half of the assertion — that the parent-declared build context resolves relative to the file that declared it — is unchanged and still the reason the case exists.

allowedDifferences.rationale: The pinned reference does not resolve `extends` at all: for this workspace `devcontainer up` fails with 'Dev container config ... is missing one of "image", "dockerFile" or "dockerComposeFile" properties', because the `build.dockerfile` is declared by the PARENT document. deacon resolves the chain and builds, so it exits 0 where the reference exits non-zero. An ahead-of-spec deacon capability recorded by ext-extends-resolution, not a defect on either side.

records.notes: The Dockerfile-with-a-Feature combination, which was a pairwise gap, observed on the two channels that can see the DIFFERENCE a Feature layer makes. The Feature layer rebuilds the image, so everything the Dockerfile established has to survive that rebuild: `chan-image` pins the Dockerfile's `ENV` and the base entrypoint on the image the container was finally created from, and `chan-injected-process` pins that the same value reaches the process alongside the configuration's `containerEnv` and under the configured non-root `containerUser`. A Feature layer built `FROM` the wrong base, or built and then not used, passes an outcome-only assertion and fails both of these. `PATH` is asserted segment-wise (the `path_env_segmented` rule), not as a string. `cwd` is deliberately NOT asserted: deacon leaves the container's `WorkingDir` empty here, and pinning that would record an uncharacterized value as an expectation.

The hook records its OWN working directory (`pwd`) into a file at an absolute path, so the assertion pins the directory that was used rather than merely the fact that something was written. Writing to a RELATIVE path would have been the shorter fixture and the worse evidence: a file that lands outside the bind mount and a hook that never ran leave the host observer with the same empty allowlist. `workspaceFolder`/`workspaceMount` fix the container path so the expected value is a constant.

`up` against a container that is ALREADY RUNNING — the pairwise combination `image` x `running`, and `running` x `features: none`, both previously gaps. The sibling metamorphic case proves re-entry does not create a second container; this one asserts what the reattached container's process context still IS, which the relationship oracle does not look at (it produces a `chan-temporal` verdict only). A reattach that silently dropped the configured `containerEnv`, or reattached to a container built before it was set, satisfies "same container, still running" and fails here.

Covers the high-risk triple `hrt-up-image-single-feature-stale-config`. The second `up` runs against a configuration that has since changed (a different `containerEnv` generation), supplied as a command-line override because the runner materializes a fixture once and does not edit it mid-case — the observable situation is identical either way. RE-POINTED after the 024 live run. The case was an `invariant-metamorphic` asserting `first-create-vs-restart`, and that relationship simply is not deacon's contract: deacon's container identity includes a configHash, so a CHANGED document is a different identity and produces a NEW container. Reuse is the dangerous branch — the container would keep the Feature layer built from the OLD configuration while every reported value came from the NEW one — so recreating is the direction worth keeping, and the metamorphic oracle had no relationship kind that could express it (the closed set is idempotence / first-create-vs-restart / resume). Asserting the relationship anyway would have pinned a behavior deacon deliberately does not have. The reference does reattach, verified directly at oracle 0.87.0; that difference is recorded as bhv-up-changed-config-recreates-container and waived by wvr-up-changed-config-recreates.

What the recreate does NOT license is leaving the superseded container RUNNING, which deacon did until [#371](https://github.com/get2knowio/deacon/issues/371). The `workspaceContainers` assertion is that fix's evidence and is the reason the case exists in this shape: `total: 2` says both generations are still THERE — the maintainer ruled 2026-08-07 that a superseded container is stopped, not removed, so its state and volumes survive for `docker start` recovery — and `running: 1` says only one of them is live. Before the fix this read `{ total: 2, running: 2 }`, measured on this fixture. The two numbers have to be asserted together: `running: 1` alone would also pass if the fix had REMOVED the old container, which is the behavior the ruling rejected, and `total: 2` alone says nothing about the leak.

The census is also what makes `status: running` above trustworthy here. Because the superseded container persists, the workspace label still matches two containers after the recreate, and the runner used to observe whichever sorted first on random hex — a coin flip that failed a draft of the differential sibling about one run in three. The runner now prefers a RUNNING container when picking what to observe, which is well-defined exactly because this case's own invariant guarantees there is only one.

WHY THE DIVERGENCE IS READ ON THE HOST FILESYSTEM, which took two wrong turns to get right and is the durable part of this case.

First, the literal observation — the reference's two `up` runs return the same containerId, deacon's return two — is not comparable across sides at all: each CLI creates its own containers, so `containerId` differs by construction on EVERY `up` case and would say nothing here.

Second, and less obvious: reading it from the created container does not work either, even though the container plainly carries the answer (deacon's `CONF_GENERATION=second` and `…/changed.json` in `devcontainer.config_file` against the reference's `first` and `…/devcontainer.json`). An earlier draft of this case observed exactly that on `chan-container-state` and passed — then failed roughly one run in three. The cause was a real interaction, not a flake to retry away: both generations carry the workspace label, both were RUNNING (https://github.com/get2knowio/deacon/issues/371), and the runner's probe sorted their ids lexicographically and observed the first — random hex, so a coin flip. #371 removed the ambiguity from the other end: exactly one generation is live now, and the runner prefers a RUNNING container when choosing what to observe. The superseded one is stopped rather than removed, so it is still THERE and the naive `.first()` would still have been a coin flip; being the live one is what makes the choice well-defined.

The hook marker has neither problem. It is captured from the host workspace, so it does not depend on which container the probe picked, and `postCreate` running exactly once per created container is the same fact the container state was standing in for — stated where a user would actually meet it. This is also the waiver's own safety argument made concrete: the container the reference hands back was provisioned from a document that no longer exists, and the work the new document asks for never happens.

The assertion pins deacon's side at `first\nsecond`, so a run in which deacon started reattaching too would fail here rather than passing as 'the two agree'. The fixture is deliberately separate from `fx-up-stale-config`: that one is shared with the spec-expectation sibling and with nothing to gain from a lifecycle hook, and it carries a local Feature this case does not observe.

What this case does NOT license is leaving the superseded container running — see #371 above, fixed 2026-08-07. The container census that proves it lives on the spec-expectation sibling (`chan-temporal`'s `workspaceContainers`) rather than here: on this side of the comparison the two CLIs legitimately DISAGREE on the total (deacon keeps the stopped generation, the reference never made one), so asserting it differentially would need a second tolerance to say what the sibling already says without one.

The boundary of the supersede sweep, and the counterpart to `case-up-stale-config-reentry`: same channel, same census, opposite answer. That case brings up ONE document twice with its content changed and asserts `{total: 2, running: 1}` — two generations, one live, which is what #371 bought. Fixes #467, and the shape it pins is the one an image-metadata case had never covered: the COLLISION.

The spec's image-metadata Merge Logic table gives each of the five lifecycle hooks a "Collected list of all <phase>Commands", with "the devcontainer.json is considered last" — so when the image's `devcontainer.metadata` and the workspace's devcontainer.json declare the SAME phase, BOTH run, the image's first. Every OTHER row of that table is last-wins, and that is how deacon folded the label in: through `ConfigMerger`, where a lifecycle command is an ordinary scalar the higher-precedence layer simply overwrites. Precedence was right; accumulation was missing.

Measured at oracle 0.87.0 before the fix, on this fixture: the reference's `lifecycle.log` read `img-onCreate` / `ws-onCreate` / `img-postCreate` / `ws-postCreate` / `img-postStart`; deacon's read only the two `ws-` lines and `img-postStart`. Both sides exit 0, so the FILE is the entire observation — no status assertion can see this.

An image hook in a phase the config does NOT declare already reached both CLIs identically; that is what #448 fixed and what `case-up-compose-image-metadata-differential` pins. `postStartCommand` is declared by the image ONLY here for exactly that reason, and it is the half a naive fix breaks: recording the image's hook as a collected layer while the merge ALSO leaves it in the singular field runs it TWICE. That is not hypothetical — it is what the first draft of the fix did, and it is why the assertion covers the WHOLE log rather than the presence of any one line. A `contains` assertion cannot see an appended duplicate.

`postCreateCommand` is declared on both sides in DIFFERENT command forms (the image's string against the config's array) so the collection cannot be quietly form-sensitive the way the compose post-create was before #460.

No `remoteUser` anywhere: the hooks run as the image's root, so nothing here depends on the `updateRemoteUserUID` remap that `case-up-compose-image-metadata-differential` is built to exercise. The last-wins half of the Merge Logic table is held by the Docker-gated tests instead — `integration_feature_lifecycle::test_up_collects_image_metadata_and_config_hooks_for_the_same_phase` declares `remoteUser` on both sides and asserts the hook's own `whoami` is the CONFIG's `root`, which is the cell that proves collecting the hooks did not turn the scalar rows into collections.

No spec-expectation twin: the fixture's base is a `:local` image built from its sibling Dockerfile by `scripts/parity/prepull-fixture-images.sh`, which only the nightly and release lanes run, so a Docker-lane twin would fail on the PR lane for a missing image rather than for a divergence — the same reason `case-up-compose-image-metadata-differential` is differential-only. The direction is pinned instead by the `assertion` carried here, evaluated against deacon's side on top of the comparison.

Only `chan-exit-code` and `chan-file-content` are observed: `chan-container-state` would drag in tolerances about labels and identity that have nothing to do with what this case is about.

STRENGTHENED after the fix landed (#467 follow-up): the fixture label carried ONE entry, which pins the collision but says nothing about the order BETWEEN metadata entries — and the merge rule is a "Collected list", so the label is an ordered array and that order is part of the claim. Closes the ORDERING half of `bhv-up-feature-install-order`, which until #417 was backed by five cases that between them declared at most ONE Feature — so the claim the behavior is named for could not fail. Three local Features each append their id to `/usr/local/share/conformance/install-order` from `install.sh`, and the case reads the file back out of the created container, so what is asserted is the sequence the installs actually ran in rather than the sequence a resolver reported.

The expected sequence is `charlie, alpha, bravo`, and every term of it is load-bearing: `overrideFeatureInstallOrder` names that order while the `features` map declares `alpha, bravo, charlie`. It therefore differs from map/declaration order, from lexicographic order (which `feature-dependencies.md` §Round Stable Sort makes the within-round tie-break, so it is what an implementation ignoring the override would produce), and from reverse map order — three Features rather than two is what rules the reversal out. `equals` rather than `contains`: `contains` cannot see an APPENDED line, which is one of the four vacuous assertions this suite has already committed once.

Measured at oracle 0.87.0: both CLIs write `charlie\nalpha\nbravo\n`. The override rule itself already has cross-CLI coverage at the RESOLUTION level (`bhv-features-override-order-*`, two `live-differential` read-configuration cases mined from upstream), so this case pins the INSTALL level on deacon's side and its dependency-order sibling carries the cross-CLI half.

The half of #417 that distinguishes the two ordering RULES. Its sibling `case-up-feature-multi-declared-order` fixes the order by declaration (`overrideFeatureInstallOrder`); here nothing declares an order and the resolved order is DERIVED, so a configuration whose declared order and resolved order coincided would not tell the two apart.

The fixture makes them differ deliberately. The `features` map declares `./features/late` first and `./features/early` second; `late` carries `installsAfter: ["./features/early"]` (a soft edge) and `dependsOn: {"./features/pulled": {}}` (a hard edge to a Feature the configuration never names). Resolution therefore has to invert the declaration AND pull in a third Feature: `early` and `pulled` are both eligible in round one and commit in the §Round Stable Sort lexicographic order, then `late` commits in round two — `early, pulled, late`. Declaration order (`late, early`) and lexicographic order over the declared set (`early, late`) are both different sequences, and neither includes `pulled` at all, so an implementation applying either rule fails here rather than passing by coincidence.

Measured at oracle 0.87.0: both CLIs write `early\npulled\nlate\n`. `case-up-feature-multi-dependency-order-differential` runs the same fixture against the reference so the agreement is enforced rather than recorded.

#476. `up --skip-post-create` defers the WHOLE lifecycle — `onCreate` and `updateContent` included — not just `postCreate` onward. deacon ran the two base phases, reading the flag off its NAME and off its own 008 FR-005. The flag is spec-silent (a CLI surface; `grep -r skip-post-create parity/spec/113500f4/` finds nothing), so the reference is the authority, and the reference is unambiguous in two independent places: its help text reads "Do not run onCreateCommand, updateContentCommand, postCreateCommand, postStartCommand or postAttachCommand and do not install dotfiles", and its bundle sets `postCreateEnabled: !skipPostCreate`, turns that into `lifecycleHook.enabled`, and invokes the ENTIRE lifecycle chain only as `params.lifecycleHook.enabled && await runPostCreateCommands(…)`.

Measured at oracle 0.87.0 on this fixture, whose five hooks all append their phase name to one file: the reference leaves no file at all; deacon's held `onCreate\nupdateContent\n`. Both sides exit 0, so the file's ABSENCE is the entire observation — which is why this asserts the `chan-filesystem` `absent` predicate rather than an exit code.

ONE operation, deliberately. `chan-filesystem` and `chan-file-content` are captured once, after ALL of a case's operations have run (`runner::execute_ops` then the `capture_channel` loop) — the `operation` field on a filesystem expectation labels the evidence, it does not choose a point in time. A second operation here would therefore observe the state AFTER it, and an `absent` predicate that a later `run-user-commands` invalidates would have looked like coverage while asserting nothing about `up`. The `run-user-commands` half — that deferral postpones the work rather than losing it — is `case-up-skip-post-create-run-user-commands-resume-differential`, where the end-of-case capture is exactly the right instant.

Spec-expectation, so it needs no oracle and runs on the `parity_docker` lane that gates pull requests and the release, which is where a regression in a lifecycle gate should be caught.

#476, the half that makes deferral safe: the deferred hooks must still RUN, and run exactly once. After `up --skip-post-create`, `run-user-commands` executes all five phases, so the append-only log holds exactly five lines in phase order. Both CLIs produce that, and their marker mechanisms differ without changing it — deacon's completion markers are host-side (`{user_data_folder}/state/<workspace-hash>/`), the reference's are container-side (`{containerDataFolder}/.<phase>CommandMarker`, keyed on the container's `createdAt`) — because neither writes a marker for a phase that never ran.

**A completed `postCreateCommand` does NOT re-run when a stopped container is brought back up; `postStartCommand` and `postAttachCommand` DO.** The single most-repeated claim in `cli.exec.base.ts` — upstream asserts it five times over different configuration shapes — and until this case NOTHING in the suite asserted it in any form. It is the property that makes the create-phase marker mechanism worth having at all: an implementation that re-ran `postCreate` on every restart would re-install, re-seed and re-migrate on every machine reboot, and would still exit 0 every time.

The observation is ONE append-only file across BOTH `up` invocations, which is what lets a single compared value carry the whole claim. Measured at oracle 0.87.0 on `fx-up-skip-post-create-phases`: both CLIs exit 0 from both operations, both reattach to the SAME container id, and both leave

    onCreate\nupdateContent\npostCreate\npostStart\npostAttach\npostStart\npostAttach\n

Seven lines, with `onCreate`, `updateContent` and `postCreate` appearing EXACTLY ONCE and `postStart`/`postAttach` twice. Every plausible wrong implementation writes a different file: re-running the create phases gives ten lines, skipping the start phases on restart gives five, and recreating the container instead of restarting it gives ten AND a different container id. `jsonSubset` on the single key is an exact-content match, so none of those pass.

ENABLED BY THE ONE CONTAINER-LIFECYCLE PRIMITIVE IN THE OPERATION VOCABULARY. `stopContainerBefore` stops this side's running containers immediately before the operation spawns, so the `up` it sits on runs against a STOPPED container rather than a fresh one. Nothing else in the model can express that: `down` REMOVES, so the next `up` recreates and `postCreate` re-runs by definition, which is the negation of the claim. The primitive is scoped to the side's own workspace label, and the two sides of a differential run in sequence over two distinct temp workspaces, so neither can stop the other's container.
